lessons.title: దయచేసి టీ (dayacēsi ṭī) — "tea, please," a word that sailed rather than walked
lessons.gloss: tea, please — Telugu's traditional word for tea travelled by sea, not by the overland road most of its neighbours took

segments.text: Two ways to say heart, done. Chapter 8's దయచేసి — please — is about to earn its keep again, in front of the drink you'd politely ask for first.

Day to day, Telugu politeness usually rides on the -అండి verb ending Chapter 8 already named as the everyday carrier — but a bare request for a drink, with no verb at all, is exactly where దయచేసి itself does the work instead.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - the word that sailed, not the word that walked

segments.text: టీ is a direct loan from English tea. English's own word traces to Hokkien (Southern Min Chinese) tê, carried west by Dutch and English sea trade through Malay teh and into Europe — the sea route.

That is the opposite road from the word most of Telugu's neighbours use. Hindi, Kannada, and Marathi all say some form of chai, which travelled overland: Mandarin chá, into Persian چای (chāy), and from Persian into North and South India alike. One drink, two Chinese dialects, two trade routes, two families of words — and Telugu's coastal contact with English trade left it holding the sea-word, ṭī, where its landlocked neighbours picked up the land-word instead.

segments.instruction: the sea route — "tê … teh … tea … ṭī"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the sea route — "tê … teh … tea … ṭī"]

segments.instruction: the land route it is not — "chá … chāy … chai"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the land route it is not — "chá … chāy … chai"]

segments.text: Say "tea, please." (Dayacēsi ṭī.) Did ṭī travel by land or by sea, and through which languages? (By sea — Hokkien tê, Malay teh, English tea.) Which word, common in Hindi, Kannada, and Marathi, took the overland road instead, and through which languages? (Chai — Mandarin chá, Persian chāy.)

lessons.title: పాలు (pālu) — "milk," where Kannada is the odd one out, not Telugu
lessons.gloss: milk — the same Proto-Dravidian word the whole family shares, with Telugu on the majority side of a regular Kannada sound law

segments.text: Ṭī showed Telugu going its own way against most of its neighbours. This word shows the opposite: Telugu sits with the majority, and one cousin stands alone.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - three sisters keep the p, one turns it to h

segments.text: పాలు (pālu) descends, unchanged, from Proto-Dravidian pāl — matching Tamil பால் (pāl) and Malayalam പാൽ (pāl) exactly. Kannada alone says ಹಾಲು (hālu), because Kannada carries a regular sound law that turns a word-initial Dravidian p- into h-: the same law that turns Tamil பத்து (pattu, "ten") into Kannada ಹತ್ತು (hattu). Telugu, Tamil, and Malayalam all keep the original p-; only Kannada shifted it.
So the pattern this chapter has been building — Telugu sometimes matching its neighbours, sometimes standing apart — flips one more time: here it is Kannada standing apart, not Telugu.

segments.instruction: the three that match — "pālu … pāl … pāl"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three that match — "pālu … pāl … pāl"]
[YOU SAY: the one that shifted — "pālu … hālu"]

segments.text: Say "milk, please." (Dayacēsi pālu.) Which three Dravidian languages keep the original p- in "milk," and which one shifts it to h-? (Telugu, Tamil, and Malayalam keep p-; Kannada alone shifts to h-, hālu.) Name one other word pair that shows the same Kannada sound law. (Tamil pattu, Kannada hattu — "ten.")
